## How the battle test decides

- An agent has the permission sets of its roles and its own, with every set they include (`IncludedPermissionSets`, permission set extensions) and without those they exclude.
- Opening a page needs Execute on the page and Read on its source table; creating a record needs Insert, changing one needs Modify. Temporary tables need nothing.
- Choosing an action runs its trigger. Every codeunit, page, or report the code calls or runs needs Execute; every table it reads or writes needs the table-data right. `Insert(true)`, `Modify(true)`, `Delete(true)`, and `Validate` run the table's triggers; events run their subscribers, whose codeunits need Execute as well.
- Every statement counts, whatever condition guards it: a step needs what its code can do, not only what it does with today's data.
- An indirect permission (lowercase, `ri`) is enough when the code that uses it has the permission itself (the `Permissions` property of the object, or of an object that calls it). `InherentPermissions` grant a right to everyone.
- A permission set that is not part of the analyzed source grants nothing on objects of the analyzed apps, except those named in `simulation.fullAccess` (default: `SUPER`).
- A right on an object of another app (Base Application, any symbol package) that the analyzed permission sets do not grant is assumed to come with that app's own permission sets, and listed on the agent's card. With `simulation.otherApps` set to `check` it is required like any other; where a permission set outside the source may grant it, the step is reported as not verifiable.
- The battle test reads the source; it does not run the app. It finds what a role cannot do for lack of permissions, not errors in the data or the logic: the AL test itself proves those.
